summary: A country on the Adriatic coast of the southwestern Balkan Peninsula, ruled by the Ottoman Empire for nearly five hundred years and declared the 'world's first atheist state' during the communist era.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: From 1385 the Ottoman Empire gradually conquered Albania, and after Skanderbeg's resistance failed in the 15th century, the land was fully incorporated into Ottoman rule around 1478. Converting to Islam reduced the jizya tax and allowed entry into the imperial bureaucracy, and from the 17th century large numbers of Albanians converted, making Sunni Islam the largest religion, found mainly in the central region and in cities.

ranking.name: Believers without a specific religion
ranking.description: In 1967 Albania was declared the 'world's first atheist state' by Enver Hoxha, and religious activity was totally banned for more than twenty years. After religious freedom was opened up in 1990, many people identified with their family's religious background but no longer had any concrete denominational affiliation, so the 2011 census showed a large number of people who 'believe in God but belong to no particular religion'.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism is concentrated in the north, centered on Shkodër; the clans of the northern mountains converted less often during the Ottoman period and enjoyed the protection of Venice and Austria. Under Hoxha Catholic clergy were severely persecuted and many priests were executed; Mother Teresa, who was born into an ethnic Albanian family, is the representative figure of contemporary Catholicism.

ranking.name: Orthodox Christianity
ranking.description: Orthodox Christianity is found mainly in the south, linked to neighboring Greece and the Byzantine tradition, and the Greek minority within the country is also mostly Orthodox. In 1922 the Albanian Orthodox Church declared its autocephaly from Constantinople, and this was recognized in 1937; in the communist era the church was likewise devastated, and in the 1990s it was rebuilt by the Greek-born Archbishop Anastasios.

ranking.name: Bektashi Order
ranking.description: The Bektashi Order is a Sufi order that originated in Anatolia in the 13th century; it was closely tied to the Ottoman Janissaries, its doctrine blends Shia elements with folk belief, and it has had a great influence in southern Albania. After Kemal dissolved the Sufi orders in Turkey in 1925, its headquarters moved to Tirana, making Albania the world center of the Bektashi.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population stems from the forced atheism policy of the communist regime of 1944-1990: in 1967 more than 2,000 mosques and churches across the country were closed or converted to other uses, and religious education was cut off. Although there has been a religious revival since the opening, some people who grew up under atheist education still hold no religious belief.

religion.background: Albania was Christianized in the Roman and Byzantine periods, and after the split between the Eastern and Western churches in 1054, the north leaned toward Roman Catholicism and the south toward Orthodoxy. From the 15th century Ottoman rule brought Islam, and by the 19th century Muslims had become the majority, while the Bektashi Order spread widely in the south. In 1967 the communist leader Hoxha declared a total ban on religion, and religious freedom was not restored until 1990. Because the three major religions coexisted for a long time and also shared the experience of persecution, Albania is known for religious tolerance, and national identity is often considered more important than religious identity.

ranking.name: Albanian
ranking.description: Albanian is an independent branch of the Indo-European family, generally thought to be related to the ancient Illyrian or Thracian language, and it is divided into the Gheg dialect of the north and the Tosk dialect of the south. The Congress of Monastir in 1908 settled on writing it in the Latin alphabet, it became the national language after independence in 1912, and in 1972 a standard language was established on the basis of the Tosk dialect. Because the country's ethnic composition is homogeneous, about 98 percent of the population speak it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Greek
ranking.description: Greek speakers are mainly the Greek minority around Gjirokastër and Sarandë in the south, an area that Greece calls 'Northern Epirus' and that was assigned to Albania when the borders were drawn in 1913. After 1990 large numbers of Albanians moved to Greece to work, and returnees also often speak Greek, but only about 1 percent of the population speak Greek as a mother tongue.

language.history: The earliest complete document in Albanian is a prayer book translated in 1555 by the Catholic priest Gjon Buzuku. In the Ottoman period it was written in Latin, Greek and Arabic scripts, the national awakening movement of the 19th century pushed for a unified script, and the Congress of Monastir in 1908 decided on the Latin alphabet. After independence in 1912, the northern Gheg dialect was for a time the more commonly used written language, but in 1972 the Tirana orthographic congress took the southern Tosk dialect as the standard. Albanians in Kosovo and North Macedonia also use the same standard language.

ranking.name: Tavë Kosi
ranking.description: Lamb and rice are roasted first, then topped with a sauce of yogurt, eggs and flour and baked in the oven, so that the surface is golden and the inside is like a savory custard.
ranking.history: Tavë kosi originated in the central city of Elbasan, where it is traditionally eaten to celebrate Summer Day (Dita e Verës) on 14 March; this spring festival comes from an ancient pagan tradition and became a national holiday after the 1990s. The yogurt and oven cooking reflect the influence of Ottoman cuisine. It is regarded as one of Albania's national dishes and often appears at family meals and festivals.

ranking.name: Byrek
ranking.description: A savory pie baked with layers of thin dough wrapped around fillings such as spinach, white cheese, minced meat or scallions; the crust is crisp and the filling moist, and it is often sold cut into squares.
ranking.history: Byrek belongs to the family of 'börek' pastries of the Ottoman Empire and entered the Balkans with Ottoman rule from the 15th century onward. In Albania, hand-rolling the dough paper-thin is regarded as an important skill of the housewife, and in the south fillings of wild greens and cheese are common. Today it is the star of breakfast and street snacks, and there are specialized byrek shops everywhere.

ranking.name: Fërgesë
ranking.description: A thick dish of green peppers, tomatoes and white cheese (or with added liver or meat) stewed in a clay pot and then baked; its texture is creamy with a slight tang.
ranking.history: The best-known version of fërgesë is that of the capital, Tirana, and it is traditionally made in a clay pot (tavë) and eaten with cornbread. Tomatoes and peppers are native to the Americas and entered the Balkans through Mediterranean trade after the 16th century, combining with the white cheese that local herding provided to form this dish. It often appears as an appetizer or at family meals in winter.

ranking.name: Qofte
ranking.description: Ground beef or lamb is mixed with onion, mint and spices and shaped into balls or logs, then charcoal-grilled or pan-fried, charred outside and tender inside, and often served with bread and yogurt sauce.
ranking.history: 'Qofte' comes from the Persian 'kufta' (pounded) and spread across the Balkans and the Middle East with the Ottoman Empire. In Albania each city has its own way of making it; in the south, for example, cheese or mint is often added. It is a common dish at grill stands and taverns (qebaptore), usually served with bread, onion and yogurt sauce.

ranking.name: Trileçe
ranking.description: Sponge cake soaked in three kinds of milk, namely milk, condensed milk and cream, topped with a layer of caramel and eaten chilled; it is moist and sweet.
ranking.history: Trileçe derives from the Latin American 'tres leches', and is generally thought to have entered Albania only after the communist regime ended in the 1990s and the country opened to the outside world, quickly becoming popular. The local version is distinguished by the caramel topping, and 'trileçe' means 'three milks'; Albanian pastry chefs later took it to Turkey, where it also became popular. Today it is the signature of dessert shops in Albania and Kosovo, showing how globalization after the opening changed contemporary food.
